walkthroughs.body_html:
Osmosis & Plant Transport — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Osmosis & Plant Transport brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Osmosis & Plant Transport.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which structure stores water in plant cells?
options: Nucleus
Permanent vacuole
Mitochondrion
Cell wall
respiration
photosynthesis
protein synthesis
mitosis

mcqs.q: In osmosis, which direction does water move?
options: Water moves towards the sugar because sugar attracts water molecules chemically.
From a region of higher water potential (less concentrated solution) to lower water potential.
Water moves from high solute concentration to low solute concentration.
Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
options: Arteries and veins both carry the same mixed blood through the body.
Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
Both move substances down a concentration gradient, but active transport is faster.
Active transport requires energy (ATP) and can move substances against the concentration gradient.

mcqs.q: Do all arteries carry oxygenated blood?
options: Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
No — the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs.
Arteries and veins both carry the same mixed blood through the body.
All arteries carry oxygenated blood and all veins carry deoxygenated blood.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Plasmodesmata”?
options: Channels between plant cells through which substances can move.
Plant cells have cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole, unlike animal cells.
Outward pressure from water in the vacuole pushing against the cell wall — keeps plant rigid.
Rigid layer of cellulose surrounding the membrane; gives shape and support.

options: Outward pressure from water in the vacuole pushing against the cell wall — keeps plant rigid.
Plant cells have cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole, unlike animal cells.
Channels between plant cells through which substances can move.

options: Outward pressure from water in the vacuole pushing against the cell wall — keeps plant rigid.

mcqs.q: A plant cell wall is ~0.1 µm thick. How many cell wall thicknesses fit across a 1 µm gap?
A plant cell is placed in pure water. What happens to it?
options: Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid.
Water leaves by osmosis and the cell becomes flaccid.
The cell bursts because plant cells have no wall.
Sugar moves out of the cell by diffusion.

mcqs.q: Wilting in a plant on a hot day is mainly caused by:
options: Cells losing water and becoming less turgid
Cells gaining too much water and bursting
The plant respiring too quickly
Too much starch in the leaves

mcqs.q: A potato strip placed in concentrated salt solution becomes soft and loses mass. The best explanation is:
options: Water left the cells by osmosis to the more concentrated solution.
Salt was actively transported into the cells.
The potato cells respired away their mass.
Water entered the cells by osmosis.

mcqs.q: Which feature of a root hair cell increases the rate at which it absorbs water?
options: A long, thin shape giving a large surface area
A thick waxy cuticle
The presence of chloroplasts
A lack of a cell membrane
